cves.summary: IP Security VPN Services Module (VPNSM) in Cisco Catalyst 6500 Series Switch and the Cisco 7600 Series Internet Routers running IOS before 12.2(17b)SXA, before 12.2(17d)SXB, or before 12.2(14)SY03 could allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (device crash and reload) via a malformed Internet Key Exchange (IKE) packet.

Bugzilla before 2.14 allows Bugzilla users to bypass group security checks by marking a bug as the duplicate of a restricted bug, which adds the user to the CC list of the restricted bug and allows the user to view the bug.

The Macro Security Model in Microsoft Excel 2000 and 2002 for Windows allows remote attackers to execute code in the Local Computer zone by embedding HTML scripts within an Excel workbook that contains an XSL stylesheet, aka "Excel XSL Stylesheet Script Execution".

The Mail Merge Tool in Microsoft Word 2002 for Windows, when Microsoft Access is present on a system, allows remote attackers to execute Visual Basic (VBA) scripts within a mail merge document that is saved in HTML format, aka a "Variant of MS00-071, Word Mail Merge Vulnerability" (CVE-2000-0788).

config_converters.py in BSCW (Basic Support for Cooperative Work) 3.x and versions before 4.06 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in the file name during filename conversion.

The default configuration of BSCW (Basic Support for Cooperative Work) 3.x and possibly version 4 enables user self registration, which could allow remote attackers to upload files and possibly join a user community that was intended to be closed.
calendar.php in vBulletin before 2.2.0 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in the command parameter.

The leafnode server in leafnode 1.9.20 to 1.9.29 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) when leafnode requests a cross-posted article to one group whose name is a prefix of another group.

Buffer overflow in AT&T WinVNC (Virtual Network Computing) server 3.3.3r7 and earlier allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via a long HTTP GET request when the DebugLevel registry key is greater than 0.
Buffer overflow in SlimServe HTTPd 1.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service, and possibly execute arbitrary commands, via a long GET request.

Buffer overflow in qDecoder library 5.08 and earlier, as used in CrazyWWWBoard, CrazySearch, and other CGI programs, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via a long MIME Content-Type header.
Buffer overflow in Trend Micro Virus Buster 2001 8.00 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service, and possibly execute arbitrary commands, via a large "To" address.
Allaire JRun 3.0 allows remote attackers to list contents of the WEB-INF directory, and the web.xml file in the WEB-INF directory, via a malformed URL that contains a "."
Lars Ellingsen guestserver.cgi allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in the "email" parameter.
Directory traversal vulnerability in Free Java Web Server 1.0 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) attack.
.reg files are associated with the Windows NT registry editor (regedit), making the registry susceptible to Trojan Horse attacks.
cci_dir in IBM U2 UniVerse 10.0.0.9 and earlier creates hard links and unlinks files as root, which allows local users to gain privileges by deleting and overwriting arbitrary files.

uvadmsh in IBM U2 UniVerse 10.0.0.9 and earlier trusts the user-supplied -uv.install command line option to find and execute the uv.install program, which allows local users to gain privileges by providing a pathname that is under control of the user.
Buffer overflow in uvadmsh in IBM U2 UniVerse 10.0.0.9 and earlier allows the uvadm user to execute arbitrary code via a long -uv.install command line argument.

X Fontserver for Truetype fonts (xfstt) 1.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via a (1) FS_QueryXExtents8 or (2) FS_QueryXBitmaps8 packet, and possibly other types of packets, with a large num_ranges value, which causes an out-of-bounds array access.
Buffer overflow in Backup and Restore Utility for Unix (BRU) 17.0 and earlier, when running setuid, allows local users to execute arbitrary code via a long command line argument.

Format string vulnerability in Backup and Restore Utility for Unix (BRU) 17.0 and earlier, when running setuid, allows local users to execute arbitrary code via format string specifiers in a command line argument.
SQL injection vulnerability in login.asp of Brooky eStore 1.0.1 through 1.0.2b allows remote attackers to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary SQL code via the (1) user or (2) pass parameters.

Microsoft Windows 2000 allows local users to bypass the policy that prohibits reusing old passwords by changing the current password before it expires, which does not enable the check for previous passwords.

Microsoft Windows 2000 running the Terminal Server 90-day trial version, and possibly other versions, does not apply group policies to incoming users when the number of connections to the SYSVOL share exceeds the maximum, e.g. with a maximum number of licenses, which can allow remote authenticated users to bypass group policies.

Multiple buffer overflows in Gaim before 0.82 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via (1) Rich Text Format (RTF) messages, (2) a long hostname for the local system as obtained from DNS, or (3) a long URL that is not properly handled by the URL decoder.

The IPv6 URI parsing routines in the apr-util library for Apache 2.0.50 and earlier allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (child process crash) via a certain URI, as demonstrated using the Codenomicon HTTP Test Tool.

Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In versions >= v2.8.2 through <= v2.11.55 and >= v3.0.0 through <= v3.7.11, the entryPoints.<name>.transport.respondingTimeouts settings — notably readTimeout, which is enabled by default at 60s — are not applied to the HTTP/3 request path. readTimeout is enforced as a deadline on the underlying TCP connection, which cannot be applied to a QUIC stream, and Traefik's HTTP/3 server is constructed without any timeout. As a result, on entry points with HTTP/3 enabled, an unauthenticated remote client that trickles request body bytes can hold a request open indefinitely and, with it, one upstream connection per request, exhausting bounded backend connection pools and causing denial of service. The issue was introduced in v2.8.2 when a quic-go API change removed the embedded http.Server that carried these timeouts. Fixed in v2.11.56 and v3.7.12.
Postfix server for Apple Mac OS X 10.3.6, when using CRAM-MD5, allows remote attackers to send mail without authentication by replaying authentication information.
Unknown vulnerability in Apple Mac OS X 10.3.6 server, when using Kerberos authentication and Cyrus IMAP allows local users to access mailboxes of other users.

Multiple buffer overflows in Oracle 9i 9 before 9.2.0.3 allow local users to execute arbitrary code by (1) setting the TIME_ZONE session parameter to a long value, or providing long parameters to the (2) NUMTOYMINTERVAL, (3) NUMTODSINTERVAL or (4) FROM_TZ functions.

The XML parser in Oracle 9i Application Server Release 2 9.0.3.0 and 9.0.3.1, 9.0.2.3 and earlier, and Release 1 1.0.2.2 and 1.0.2.2.2, and Database Server Release 2 9.2.0.1 and later, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU and memory consumption) via a SOAP message containing a crafted DTD.

The WP Photo Album Plus plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authenticated Command Injection in all versions up to, and including, 9.3.02.002 via the `value` parameter of the `update-photo` AJAX action. This is due to insufficient shell escaping within the `wppa_image_magick_a()` function, where the attacker-controlled `value` parameter is concatenated raw — without `escapeshellarg()` — into an ImageMagick command string before being passed to `exec()`; further, `wppa_decode()` actively restores percent-encoded shell metacharacters (e.g., `%26`→`&`, `%23`→`#`) rather than stripping them, allowing crafted payloads to survive sanitization and break out of the ImageMagick argument context. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers holding the plugin-defined `wppa_upload` capability to execute arbitrary operating-system commands as the web-server user, achieving full remote code execution on the underlying server. Exploitation requires ImageMagick to be enabled on the server; the `wppa_upload` capability is a plugin-level privilege that site administrators may grant to lower-privileged WordPress roles via the plugin's Users settings, broadening the pool of potential attackers beyond administrators.

The YaySMTP – WP Mail SMTP with Email Logs, Tracking & Reports plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Upload in all versions up to, and including, 2.7.7 via the putFile function. This is due to insufficient file type validation in the putFile function, as sanitize_file_name() does not strip executable extensions and no allow-list, MIME check, or safe-extension rename is applied. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to upload files that may be executable, which makes remote code execution possible. The only server-side guard is a .htaccess file containing 'Require all denied' written by writeGuards(), which is silently ignored by nginx and by Apache configured with AllowOverride None, meaning RCE is fully achievable on those server configurations.

The Subscribe to Comments WordPress plugin before 2.3.3 does not sign or validate a cookie it trusts to identify a commenter, allowing unauthenticated attackers to disclose a subscriber's management key and silently alter that subscriber's subscriptions.

Mattermost versions 11.10.x <= 11.10.0, 11.7.x <= 11.7.9, 11.9.x <= 11.9.1, 11.8.x <= 11.8.5 fail to validate the combination of guest and admin scheme roles which allows an authenticated attacker to escalate a guest account to team or channel admin via a crafted PUT request to the member roles API endpoint.. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00752
Sun Ray Server Software (SRSS) 1.3, when Non-Smartcard Mobility (NSCM) is enabled, allows remote attackers to login as another user by running dtlogin from a system that supports the XDMCP client.
A certain ActiveX control in Symantec Norton AntiVirus 2004 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (resource consumption) and possibly execute arbitrary programs.
UltraBoard.pl or UltraBoard.cgi CGI scripts in UltraBoard 1.6 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a pathname string that includes a dot dot (..) and ends with a null byte.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: Reset write verifier when async COPY writeback fails

Async COPY captures nn->writeverf at request time and reports it to
the client via CB_OFFLOAD after the worker kthread completes. When
the post-copy vfs_fsync_range() or filemap_check_wb_err() in
_nfsd_copy_file_range() reports an error, the worker correctly
leaves NFSD4_COPY_F_COMMITTED clear so that CB_OFFLOAD encodes
wr_stable_how as NFS_UNSTABLE, but the server's write verifier is
not rotated.

A client that receives NFS_UNSTABLE in CB_OFFLOAD follows up with
COMMIT to make the copied data durable. With the verifier
unchanged, COMMIT returns the same value the client just received
via CB_OFFLOAD, and the client concludes the copy is durable --
silently dropping the data whose writeback in fact failed. This
violates the UNSTABLE+COMMIT durability contract (RFC 7862 section
15.1, RFC 8881 section 18.32) and matches the bug just fixed in
nfsd_vfs_write() and nfsd_commit().

Rotate nn->writeverf at the writeback-failure site. The async COPY
worker has no svc_rqst, so commit_reset_write_verifier() is not
available here; calling nfsd_reset_write_verifier() directly
mirrors the trace-less reset already used by
nfsd_file_check_write_error() for the same purpose. Filter out
-EAGAIN and -ESTALE, matching commit_reset_write_verifier(), since
neither indicates a durable-storage failure.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

lockd, nfsd: RCU-protect nlmsvc_ops dispatch

nlmsvc_ops is published by nfsd_lockd_init() and cleared by
nfsd_lockd_shutdown() with plain stores, while lockd dereferences
it unguarded from dispatch sites in fs/lockd/svcsubs.c. The pointer
targets nfsd's .rodata and the fopen/fclose callbacks live in nfsd's
.text, so a stale load after rmmod nfsd results in either a NULL
deref or a module-text use-after-free.

Declare nlmsvc_ops as __rcu, publish via rcu_assign_pointer(), clear
via RCU_INIT_POINTER() + synchronize_rcu(). Add a struct module
*owner field to nlmsvc_binding and pin the module across indirect
calls with try_module_get/module_put. When the binding is torn down,
fall back to fput() to avoid leaking struct file references.

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

## Technical details

The pod handlers pass `podname` and `podnamespace` query values to `getPod` and `listPodEvents` in `frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts`. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

[PR #12295](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12295) changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with `isAllowedResourceName`. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

## Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as `ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend`. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to **KFP 2.15.0 or later**.

The fix merged on October 10, 2025, in commit [fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/commit/fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e). It is first present in the **2.15.0** release, published November 25, 2025.

The affected range is recorded as `< 2.15.0`. The original introduction version and separate maintenance-branch backports have not been established. These are KFP component versions, not Kubeflow platform or Python SDK versions.

## Distinction from existing artifact XSS

[CVE-2023-6571](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7rvc-xw75-43jf), tracked in the repository as [GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r), documents reflection of the artifact `source` parameter in an unknown-storage-source error.

This report concerns different handlers and error construction: pod information and pod events. The artifact-source fix in [PR #9844](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/9844), released in 2.0.2, did not repair these pod responses. They required the later change in #12295.

This independently fixable pod-route defect is tracked as CVE-2026-88986. It does not broaden CVE-2023-6571 or absorb artifact-content rendering and other XSS reports.

## Attribution

**@pwny0** submitted this report on September 23, 2023, and retains the reporter credit.

**@JerT33** authored the remediation in PR #12295. Fix attribution is separate from vulnerability-report attribution.

## Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the `page_token` pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in [GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9). Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

## Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

Authentication and authorization requirements depend on deployment configuration. In multi-user deployments, the attacker must pass the applicable endpoint authorization checks. A single-user deployment that exposes the API without an authentication layer may be reachable without credentials.

The submitted evidence establishes a confidentiality issue. Database modification was not demonstrated; this advisory does not claim arbitrary database writes.

## Technical details

Pagination tokens are base64-encoded JSON, not trusted server-side state. Before the fix, token deserialization accepted structural fields such as key and sort identifiers without sufficient validation before SQL construction.

The reports describe complementary paths through this defect:

- **Pipeline listing:** the original report demonstrated injection through `KeyFieldName`.
- **Run listing:** the later report documented `SortByFieldName` reaching query construction in both the v1beta1 and v2beta1 APIs, including metric joins, selected column aliases, ordering, and column propagation through resource-reference and task joins.

These paths share the unvalidated pagination-token boundary. Review of the later report and its discussion identified no reported path left unresolved by the merged fix.

## Remediation

Upgrade the Kubeflow Pipelines API server to **2.17.0 or later**.

[PR #13127](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13127), included in 2.17.0, validates token identifiers and filter keys before query construction. It also separates user-facing metric names from SQL identifiers, uses a fixed metric-column alias, and parameterizes the metric-name join condition.

The PR additionally addresses first-page metric sorting without a pagination token. That additional protection is part of the remediation; the duplicate determination here concerns the page-token claims actually submitted in the two reports, not merely their inclusion in the same PR.

The original report identified its deployment as **Kubeflow 1.7**, which should not be interpreted as a verified Kubeflow Pipelines component-version boundary. The later report identified **KFP 2.16.0**. These are reported affected environments, not an established introduction version.

## Attribution and report history

- **@phisch1991 and @k0rti:** credited reporters of the original pipeline-listing SQL injection submitted on December 13, 2023.
- **BugBunny.ai (@bugbunny-research):** submitted the later report on April 1, 2026, documenting the run-listing and metric-query paths in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. This acknowledges that specific contribution without implying authorship of the 2023 report.
- **Cyber Nagle:** authored the merged remediation in PR #13127.

GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9 is consolidated here for vulnerability tracking. Its submission and reporter credit remain preserved on that advisory; closure as a duplicate does not characterize the report as invalid.

## Summary

In Kiwi TCMS version 16.1, the fix for CVE-2026-54724 (open redirect via unvalidated `next` parameter) in the account confirmation endpoint is incomplete. The validation uses `startswith("/")` to check if the redirect URL is local, but this is bypassed by protocol-relative URLs like `//evil.com` which start with `/` but redirect the browser to an external attacker-controlled domain. 16.1’s incomplete mitigation still allows protocol-relative destinations and earlier releases lack the mitigation.

## Vulnerable Code

In `tcms/kiwi_auth/views.py`, the `Confirm` view (line ~113):

    def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
        if not self.url.startswith("/"):
            self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

The check `startswith("/")` passes for `//evil.com` because it begins with `/`, but browsers interpret `//evil.com` as a protocol-relative URL that redirects to `https://evil.com` (or `http://evil.com` depending on the current page's protocol).

## Proof of Concept

    GET /confirm/<activation_key>/?next=//evil.com/phishing HTTP/1.1
    Host: kiwi.example.com

Response:

    HTTP/1.1 302 Found
    Location: //evil.com/phishing

The browser follows the redirect to `https://evil.com/phishing`.

Verification:

    >>> url = "//evil.com/phishing"
    >>> url.startswith("/")
    True  # passes the check!

## Impact

An attacker can craft a confirmation link that, after the user confirms their account, redirects them to a phishing page. This is useful for:

- Credential phishing (fake login page on attacker domain)
- Malware delivery after trusted action
- Social engineering (user trusts the link because it's from the legitimate Kiwi TCMS instance)

The attack requires sending a crafted activation link to a user who is registering, or intercepting/predicting the activation key.

## Suggested Fix

Use Django's `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme()` utility instead of a simple `startswith` check:

    from django.utils.http import url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme

    def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
        if not url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(
            self.url,
            allowed_hosts={self.request.get_host()},
            require_https=self.request.is_secure(),
        ):
            self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

This properly rejects protocol-relative URLs, absolute URLs to other hosts, and other bypass patterns.

Fixed in Version 16.2
SQL injection vulnerability in redir_url.php in w-Agora 4.1.6a allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands via the key parameter.

### Impact

The LoginRadius backend did not validate OAuth state during the authentication flow.

Applications using this backend were vulnerable to login CSRF. An attacker could cause a victim's browser session to complete authentication using an attacker-controlled LoginRadius token, making the victim authenticated as the attacker's LoginRadius identity.

The issue affects only applications using the LoginRadius backend.

### Patches

The issue has been fixed by enabling callback state validation for the LoginRadius backend.

Users should upgrade to a patched version.

Fix:

* https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1808

### Workarounds

Applications that cannot upgrade immediately should disable the LoginRadius backend by removing it from `SOCIAL_AUTH_AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`.

There is no complete workaround while continuing to use the vulnerable backend.

### Credits

Reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting by Liyi Zhou, Ziyue Wang, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu from the University of Sydney security research team.

Reporter references:

* https://lzhou1110.github.io/
* https://zyy0530.github.io/
* https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/

``` ============================================================================ Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id) Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629 in next_object_id() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely *declares* a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies. The cause is `PdfParser.next_object_id()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`, which finds the next free id by computing `max(self.xref_table.keys())`. `XrefTable.keys()` rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. `PdfImagePlugin._save()` calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for `n_frames` frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because `n_frames` is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's `acTL` count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises `OSError` only after the full delay. The precondition is that the application calls `im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True)` on the attacker's file; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in `XrefTable` makes the save linear. ## Details Saving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (`im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)`) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far. A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not): | frames | GIF size | `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)` | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 2 000 | 30 KB | 1.1 s | | | 8 000 | 120 KB | 14.7 s | | | 16 000 | 240 KB | 70 s | 60 MB | | 32 000 | 480 KB | 262 s | 95 MB | | 48 000 | 720 KB | still running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min) | | Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. `cProfile` of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of `PdfParser.next_object_id` (8.9 s inside `XrefTable.keys`, 3.9 s inside `max`); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly. The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written: ```python # src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259 (_save) for im in ims: im_number_of_pages = 1 if save_all: im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) … for i in range(im_number_of_pages): image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info: image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) ``` `n_frames` comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on `n_frames` before any frame is seeked, and for APNG `n_frames` is the `num_frames` value declared in the `acTL` chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above `0x80000000` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720`). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for `P` images with transparency) calls per frame lands here: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634 def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: try: # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) except ValueError: reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178 (XrefTable) def keys(self) -> set[int]: return ( set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys()) ) | set(self.new_entries.keys()) ``` `_save` passes `offset=0`, so every reserved id is inserted into `xref_table.new_entries`. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a difference and a union, and then `max()` scans the result — O(k) work to produce the integer k. Summed over 3N calls this is O(N²): for 48 000 frames, 144 002 calls over sets growing to 144 002 elements, on the order of 10¹⁰ set-element operations, all spent before `_write_image` is reached for the first frame. Nothing on this path consults `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (the frames are 1×1) and nothing raises; for the GIF the save eventually completes and produces a valid PDF, and for the declared-only APNG it raises `OSError` only once the id loop has finished and the first missing frame is seeked. This reservation scheme was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` ("issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs", 2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0; before it, the writer numbered objects arithmetically. For contrast, `write_obj(ref, …)` with an already-reserved `ref` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:548-555`) only does a dict store, which is why the page-writing phase that follows is linear; the super-linear cost is entirely in how the next free id is computed. ## Impact The precondition is that the application saves the attacker's image as PDF with `save_all=True`; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. An application that converts uploaded images to PDF this way — the documented way to get one page per frame from animated GIF/APNG/WebP or multi-page TIFF input — can have a worker held at 100 % CPU for about 10 minutes by a 720 KB GIF, about 4½ minutes by a 480 KB one, with the cost continuing to grow quadratically with upload size. With APNG the file size does not matter at all: a 125-byte file declaring N frames in `acTL` drives the same quadratic loop, up to the 2³¹ cap. The attacker controls only the file bytes; no unusual dimensions, modes or options are needed, memory use stays under 100 MB so memory limits do not intervene, and the decompression-bomb guard is not applicable. The consequence is denial of service of the process performing the conversion. Single-image PDF saves, and `save_all` saves of images with tens or hundreds of frames, are unaffected in practice. This is the same family as earlier accidentally-quadratic parsing issues fixed in Pillow (e.g. CVE-2021-28677, EPS `readline`), but on the PDF *writer* side, reached only through a save rather than on open, and driven by frame count rather than by line structure. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. Run it with the Python that has Pillow installed (`./repro`). It uses under 100 MB of RAM and writes no files. **Input.** Two kinds of file are built in memory, each with 2 000 and 8 000 frames: - `gif(n)`: a valid animated GIF — a `GIF89a` header with a 1×1 logical screen and a 2-colour global palette, then `n` copies of one 15-byte frame (a 1×1 image descriptor plus the LZW data for one pixel), then the trailer (30 and 120 KB). The only unusual thing about it is how many frames it has. - `apng(n)`: a 125-byte APNG — a 1×1 greyscale `IHDR`, an `acTL` chunk declaring `n` frames, one `fcTL`, one `IDAT` and `IEND`. Only the first frame exists; the other `n − 1` are merely declared. **Action.** Each file goes through what an upload-to-PDF converter would do: `Image.open(BytesIO(data))`, then `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)`, timed with `time.process_time()`. For the APNG the save raises `OSError` once the writer tries to seek to the second frame; that happens after the id-reservation loop has run for all `n` declared frames, so the exception is caught and the CPU time up to it is recorded. **Expected output** (stock build at this commit): ``` GIF frames= 2000 file= 30020 B save CPU= 1.03s result=ok GIF frames= 8000 file=120020 B save CPU= 11.68s result=ok GIF: 4x frames -> 11.3x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) APNG frames= 2000 file= 125 B save CPU= 0.65s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG frames= 8000 file= 125 B save CPU= 10.48s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG: 4x frames -> 16.1x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) BUG ``` A linear save would take about 4× as long for 4× the frames; here the GIF save grows ~11× and the APNG save ~16×, the latter with the file size fixed at 125 bytes. The script prints `BUG` when the save CPU for either format grows at least 8× for 4× the frames (twice the linear expectation), otherwise `OK`. Extending the same curve gives the figures in the table above: about 70 s at 16 000 frames (240 KB GIF), and about 10 minutes for a 720 KB file. With the attached patch applied, the GIF save takes 0.32 s / 1.20 s (3.7×) and the APNG save 0.01 s / 0.03 s, and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix Make `next_object_id()` O(1) by tracking the highest object id ever stored in `XrefTable` instead of rebuilding the key set on every call. The attached patch does this in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`: ```diff a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ class XrefTable: self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ class PdfParser: def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` `existing_entries` is only ever populated through `__setitem__` (from `read_xref_table` / `read_prev_trailer`), so the counter also covers ids read from an existing file in `append=True` mode. The one behavioural difference: when the highest-numbered existing object has just been deleted (`del_root()` / `rewrite_pages()` in append mode), the current code hands that id out again with generation 0, whereas the patch moves on to the next unused id — the more conservative choice for an xref table, and the one the existing `TODO: support reuse of deleted objects` comment points at. With the patch applied and Pillow rebuilt, the 16 000-frame save drops from ~70 s to ~2.5 s, fresh PDF output is unchanged, `Tests/test_file_pdf.py` and `Tests/test_pdfparser.py` pass, and the reproducer prints `OK`. An alternative limited to the writer would be to reserve the `3 × number_of_pages` ids in `PdfImagePlugin._save()` arithmetically from a single `next_object_id()` call, but fixing the allocator also covers `write_obj(None, …)` callers. The patch does not address a separate, linear issue: `PdfImagePlugin._save()` still trusts `n_frames` before any frame is decoded, so a tiny file whose format reports a declared-only frame count (APNG `acTL` up to 2³¹) still makes it loop `3 × n_frames` times before the first failing seek. Reserving ids per successfully seeked frame, or validating `n_frames` in such plugins, would close that. ## The patch Track the highest object ID in XrefTable so PdfParser.next_object_id() is O(1) instead of rebuilding and scanning the key set Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py index 672557190..82ebfb867 100644 a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ -133,12 +133,15 @@ class XrefTable: ) # object ID => (offset, generation) self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ -624,11 +627,8 @@ class PdfParser: self.orig_pages = self.pages[:] def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,791 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # PDF save_all is O(frames^2): PdfParser.next_object_id() does max(XrefTable.keys()), # and keys() rebuilds sets of every id reserved so far, 3 calls per frame. # (a) valid 1x1 animated GIF, 15 bytes/frame; (b) 125-byte APNG whose acTL merely # *declares* N frames - ids are reserved for all N before the first seek fails. import io, struct, time, zlib from PIL import Image def gif(n): return (b"GIF89a\x01\x00\x01\x00\x80\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xff\xff\xff" + b"\x2c\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00\x00\x02\x02\x44\x01\x00" * n + b"\x3b") def apng(n): def chunk(t, d): return struct.pack(">I", len(d)) + t + d + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + d)) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 1, 1, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"acTL", struct.pack(">II", n, 0)) + chunk(b"fcTL", struct.pack(">IIIIIHHBB", 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"\x00\x00")) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def save_pdf(data): im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) t = time.process_time() try: im.save(io.BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True) res = "ok" except OSError as e: # APNG: frames don't exist, fails *after* the id loop res = f"OSError({e})" return time.process_time() - t, res bug = False for name, make in (("GIF", gif), ("APNG", apng)): t = {} for n in (2000, 8000): data = make(n) t[n], res = save_pdf(data) print(f"{name:4} frames={n:5} file={len(data):6} B save CPU={t[n]:6.2f}s result={res}") growth = t[8000] / t[2000] print(f"{name}: 4x frames -> {growth:.1f}x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x)") if growth >= 8: bug = True print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```
